knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let clients \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) retain local data governed by distributions \(\mathcal D_i\). Let \(f_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim\mathcal D_i}[\ell_i(w;\xi)]\) and let weights \(p_i\ge0\) satisfy \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinator-mediated optimization of a shared finite-dimensional model under persistent data locality, heterogeneous clients, and possibly partial participation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Federated optimization is the problem \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i f_i(w)\), or its population-client analogue, under the information constraint that raw client data remain local and the optimization protocol exchanges model states, updates, statistics, or protected messages rather than pooling the underlying samples. At communication round \(t\), only a subset \(S_t\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) may participate; participating clients may perform multiple local computations before transmitting, and a coordinator combines the returned information. The mathematical objective and the communication-participation process are both part of the problem specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Federated optimization minimizes a weighted aggregate of client risks while client data remain at their sources. Clients compute from local data and communicate permitted updates or statistics, typically through a coordinator. Participation can vary by round, and clients may perform several local computations between communication events. The definition requires both a global objective and an information pattern; merely partitioning an ordinary centralized dataset does not by itself specify a federated deployment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical shared-model objective is \(\min_{w\in W}\sum_i p_i\mathbb E_{\xi\sim\mathcal D_i}[\ell_i(w;\xi)]\) subject to local data access and protocol-defined communication.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite local datasets \(D_i\), one may take \(f_i(w)=|D_i|^{-1}\sum_{\xi\in D_i}\ell_i(w;\xi)\).
special_cases_latex: Choosing \(p_i=|D_i|/\sum_j|D_j|\) yields the empirical risk over the union of disjoint local samples without physically pooling them.
Full participation has \(S_t=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) at every round.
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonidentical \(\mathcal D_i\) generally produce distinct local objectives even though all clients optimize a shared parameter.
boundary_notes: Data locality alone does not guarantee privacy, security, or robustness.
Personalized and model-heterogeneous federation require objectives with client-specific parameters.

children.title: Federated Optimization Settings
children.top_down_role: Deployment and objective regimes distinguished by population scale, data alignment, and coordination.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a finite or measurable client population, let \(P\) be a probability law on clients, and for each client \(i\) let \(\mathcal D_i\) be a local data law and \(f_i:W\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) its local objective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-model federated objectives covering finite-client and population-client formulations; topology and algorithm are specified separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federated optimization problem is the tuple \((W,\mathcal I,P,\{\mathcal D_i,f_i\}_{i\in\mathcal I},\mathfrak A)\), where \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is the parameter domain and \(\mathfrak A\) is an admissible information-access and coordination model, with objective \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\). In the finite case, \(P(i)=p_i\) and \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i f_i(w)\). The access model requires evaluation or estimation of \(f_i\) to occur at client \(i\) and specifies which clients may be queried and which messages may be communicated. A solution is any \(w_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{w\in W}F(w)\), when the argmin is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A federated optimization problem specifies a parameter domain, a client population and its weighting law, each client's local data and objective, and the permitted access and coordination pattern. Its global objective is the expectation of the local objective over clients. For finitely many clients this is a weighted sum. The formal problem therefore distinguishes what is optimized from how local information may be accessed; an algorithm is not part of the solution definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_\star\) solves the problem exactly when \(w_\star\in W\) and \(F(w_\star)=\inf_{w\in W}\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The finite-population form is recovered by the discrete law \(P=\sum_i p_i\delta_i\).
special_cases_latex: Uniform client weighting uses \(p_i=1/n\); sample weighting uses weights proportional to local dataset sizes.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing \(P\) changes the optimization problem even if every local objective is unchanged.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require convexity or differentiability.
A deployment label such as cross-device or cross-silo adds population and availability assumptions, not a different algebraic minimizer definition by itself.

notation.meaning: client weighting or sampling law defining the target objective

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source supports the complete tuple-based problem specification.

children.title: Cross-Device Federated Optimization
children.top_down_role: Large intermittent populations of resource-constrained clients.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Device Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federated objective with sampled participation from a large, intermittently available client population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-device federated optimization minimizes
\[F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w),\qquad F_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P_i}[\ell(w;\xi)],\]
over a shared parameter \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), where the client population is large and each communication round accesses only an available subset \(S_t\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\). Client data remain local, participation may be intermittent, and the server update is computed from messages produced by clients in \(S_t\), rather than from simultaneous access to all local objectives or datasets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A large population of intermittently available devices jointly minimizes a weighted objective through sampled client participation while retaining data locally.
assumptions_latex: All clients optimize a common parameter space \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-device regime is characterized by the weighted federated objective and partial, availability-dependent client participation.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the cross-device regime definition.
standard_field_rationale: sampled intermittent participation in a large client population is the conventional cross-device distinction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but no source with a locator supports the regime characterization. Requiring a strict subset in every round is stronger than the usual cross-device distinction and needs confirmation or correction from an authoritative federated-learning source.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal I\) be a large population of end-user devices, with client law \(P\), local objectives \(f_i:W\to\mathbb R\), and round-dependent available and selected sets \(A_t,S_t\subseteq\mathcal I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-model federation over a large, intermittently available, resource-constrained device population coordinated in communication rounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cross-device federated optimization is the population objective \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\) under the regime in which \(\mathcal I\) is large, an individual device need not be continuously addressable, and each round uses a finite selected subset \(S_t\subseteq A_t\subseteq\mathcal I\). Device \(i\) can evaluate its local objective only while available, raw data remain on that device, and the protocol must define selection probabilities \(q_{i,t}=\Pr(i\in S_t\mid i\in A_t,\mathcal H_t)\) or an equivalent sampling rule. Resource restrictions limit local computation, storage, energy, or communication per participation event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-device federated optimization targets the client-population risk across many end-user devices. Devices are intermittently available and only a finite subset participates in any round. Local data remain on devices, while the protocol communicates permitted updates. A complete mathematical specification includes the target client distribution and the availability and selection process, because observed participants may not represent the target population.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target remains \(\min_w\mathbb E_{i\sim P}[f_i(w)]\), while admissible observations at round \(t\) are restricted to the selected available set \(S_t\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a finite but very large device population, \(P\) may be a discrete distribution and the expectation becomes a weighted sum.
special_cases_latex: Uniform sampling from currently available devices has \(q_{i,t}=m_t/|A_t|\) when exactly \(m_t\) devices are selected.
immediate_consequences_latex: Availability-biased selection can target an objective different from the intended law \(P\) unless corrected.
boundary_notes: Large population size is a deployment regime, not a precise universal numeric threshold.
Persistent institutional participants are normally classified as cross-silo rather than cross-device.

notation.meaning: devices selected to participate at round t

review_flags: No inspected source locator supports the deployment-specific conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-device federated optimization regime
unreliable edge-client participation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Edge-client participation is unreliable when at least one repeatedly eligible device has a nontrivial conditional probability of becoming unavailable before its round response is delivered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For device set \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\), let \(A_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that device \(i\), if invited in round \(t\), remains available through the response deadline. Participation is unreliable when some recurrent device has genuinely random availability: there exist \(i\) and infinitely many rounds \(t\) for which \(0<\mathbb{P}(A_{i,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)<1\). Any realized responding set \(S_t\) must then satisfy \(S_t\subseteq\{i:A_{i,t}=1\}\); no fixed client set is guaranteed to respond in every round.
assumptions_latex: \(N<\infty\) is the eligible device population for the modeled deployment interval.
\(\mathcal H_t\) contains all information revealed before round-\(t\) availability is realized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists i:\left|\left\{t:0<\mathbb{P}(A_{i,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)<1\right\}\right|=\infty.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-availability model for cross-device federated rounds.

notation.meaning: Indicator that invited device i remains available through the round deadline.
Devices whose valid responses are received in round t.

review_flags: A federated-systems source is required for this precise conditional-availability formulation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-probability criterion is a bespoke formalization not supported by a cited federated-systems source, and “recurrent device” is not formally defined. Moreover, randomness of one device does not imply that no nonempty fixed set of other clients is guaranteed to respond in every round.

knowledge_statements.title: large-client-population regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deployment is in the large-client-population regime when the eligible population grows while each round samples an asymptotically vanishing fraction of it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a sequence of federated systems indexed by the eligible population size \(N\to\infty\). If \(S_{N,t}\subseteq[N]\) is the set participating in round \(t\), define the conditional participation fraction by \(q_{N,t}=\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]/N\). The sequence is in the large-client-population regime when, for every fixed round \(t\), \(q_{N,t}\to0\). Thus the server interacts with an asymptotically negligible fraction of the eligible population in each fixed round, even if the cohort size grows.
assumptions_latex: The systems have eligible populations \([N]\) with \(N\to\infty\).
The conditional expected cohort size \(\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall t\text{ fixed},\qquad \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}[|S_{N,t}|\mid\mathcal H_{N,t}]}{N}=0.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic cross-device regime with a vanishing sampled fraction per round.

notation.meaning: Participating cohort in round t of the N-client system.
Information available before sampling the round-t cohort.

review_flags: An authoritative cross-device federated-learning source is required for the chosen asymptotic definition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Cross-device systems commonly have large client populations and small per-round cohorts, but the proposed asymptotic definition requiring a vanishing conditional expected fraction for every fixed round is not established by a cited source. An authoritative source is needed to determine whether this is the intended local meaning rather than a stronger derived regime.

children.top_down_role: Smaller populations of persistent institutional participants.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Silo Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federated objective over a small set of persistent institutional clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-silo federated optimization minimizes
\[F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w),\qquad F_i(w)=\mathbb E_{\xi\sim P_i}[\ell(w;\xi)],\]
over a shared parameter \(w\in\mathbb R^d\), where the clients are a comparatively small, fixed collection of institutions. Each client maintains a local dataset and computational service, identities persist across rounds, and the protocol may schedule all clients or a known subset while exchanging model-derived messages instead of raw records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed, relatively small group of persistent institutions optimizes a weighted shared objective without pooling their raw datasets.
assumptions_latex: The institutional client set is fixed during the optimization horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The cross-silo regime has persistent identified participants jointly optimizing \(F\) while retaining their local records.

notation.meaning: institution i's local population or empirical objective

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the cross-silo regime definition.
standard_field_rationale: persistent institutional participants are the conventional cross-silo distinction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role and persistent-institutional-client description fit the leaf, but the record has no cited source or inspectable locator supporting the exact cross-silo characterization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) index organizations, each controlling a persistent data silo with objective \(f_i:W\to\mathbb R\), and let fixed weights \(p_i\ge0\) sum to one.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation among a comparatively small, stable set of institutionally administered participants with persistent identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Cross-silo federated optimization is the problem \(\min_{w\in W}F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i f_i(w)\) under an organizational regime in which participants have persistent identities and administer separate data silos, raw records are not centrally pooled, and communication occurs through an agreed coordinator or inter-silo protocol. The participant set and weights are ordinarily stable over the optimization horizon; participation requirements, authentication, and message permissions are part of the admissible coordination model. Temporary failures may occur, but intermittent anonymous participation is not the defining population model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-silo federated optimization minimizes a weighted objective across separately administered organizations. The organizations retain their raw records and have stable identities, so the participant set and objective weights can normally be specified explicitly. Communication may use a coordinator or another agreed protocol. Occasional failures do not alter the defining feature that the federation consists of persistent institutional data holders.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical target is the fixed finite sum \(\min_{w\in W}\sum_i p_i f_i(w)\) under persistent silo-local data access.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With local empirical risks and sample-proportional \(p_i\), the objective equals the pooled empirical risk algebraically while retaining silo-local access.
special_cases_latex: Full participation requires every silo to contribute in each communication round.
immediate_consequences_latex: Stable identities permit client-specific constraints or weights to remain attached to the same organizations across rounds.
boundary_notes: No universal numerical cutoff separates cross-silo from cross-device federation.
Cross-silo does not imply identical local distributions or equal computational capacity.

notation.meaning: fixed target weight assigned to silo i

review_flags: No inspected source locator supports the cross-silo regime definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Cross-silo federated optimization regime
organizational data-silo setting
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent organizations jointly minimize a weighted aggregate objective while each organization retains custody of the raw data defining its local objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An organizational data-silo setting consists of persistent organizations \(k\in[K]\), each controlling a private dataset or distribution and a local objective \(f_k:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\). The shared optimization problem is \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x)\), where \(F(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k f_k(x)\), \(a_k>0\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k=1\). Computation may exchange model parameters, sufficient statistics, or updates, but each organization retains custody of its raw examples rather than pooling them centrally.
assumptions_latex: \(K<\infty\) organizations have stable identities across optimization rounds.
All local objectives share the parameter domain \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
The aggregation weights satisfy \(a_k>0\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}F(x),\qquad F(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k f_k(x),\quad \sum_{k=1}^{K}a_k=1.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-silo federated objective distributed among persistent organizations.

notation.meaning: Objective induced by organization k's private data.
Positive aggregation weight of organization k.

review_flags: The supplied source hints do not document the cross-silo organizational deployment definition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The weighted federated objective is mathematically coherent and the definition fits the cross-silo leaf, but no citation supports the asserted organizational persistence, data-custody, and permitted-message characteristics as the exact deployment definition.

knowledge_statements.title: high-availability client assumption
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every persistent silo remains available through each round with conditional probability at least a prescribed high threshold; perfect availability is the threshold-one special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_{k,t}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate that organizational client \(k\) is available for the entirety of round \(t\), and let \(\mathcal H_t\) be the pre-round history. For a prescribed \(\delta\in[0,1)\), the high-availability assumption holds when \(\mathbb{P}(A_{k,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)\geq1-\delta\) almost surely for every client and round. The full-participation availability idealization is the special case \(\delta=0\); availability alone does not require the server to select every available client.
assumptions_latex: The client set \([K]\) is persistent across rounds.
Availability is measured from round invitation through the response deadline.
\(\delta\in[0,1)\) is fixed independently of the client and round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{k\in[K],\,t\geq0}\mathbb{P}(A_{k,t}=1\mid\mathcal H_t)\geq1-\delta\quad\text{almost surely}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform conditional availability condition for persistent cross-silo clients.

notation.meaning: Round-long availability indicator for silo k.
Information revealed before round t begins.

review_flags: The numerical meaning of high availability is deployment-dependent.
A cross-silo federated-learning source is required for the uniform conditional formulation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The uniform conditional lower bound is mathematically well formed, but neither the threshold parameter nor this probability model is a standard meaning of “high availability” without a source. The intended cross-silo assumption may instead be deterministic availability, frequent participation, or bounded dropout.

children.title: Federated Data Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Federation distinguished by sample, feature, and task alignment.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For client \(i\), let \(R_i\) be its entity or sample identifiers, \(C_i\) its observed feature coordinates, and \(T_i\) its prediction-task or label coordinates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A set-theoretic taxonomy of federations by alignment of entities, features, and tasks; privacy-preserving record linkage is outside the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The alignment signature of a federation is the pattern of overlap among \(\{R_i\}\), \(\{C_i\}\), and \(\{T_i\}\). A federation is horizontally aligned when clients share a common feature and task space, \(C_i=C\) and \(T_i=T\), while their entity sets are principally disjoint or only weakly overlapping. It is vertically aligned when participating clients refer to a materially overlapping entity set but hold distinct feature blocks, so \(R_i\approx R\) and the \(C_i\) are complementary. It is transfer or task-heterogeneous when both entity and feature overlap are limited or when task spaces differ, requiring an explicit relation among client representations or tasks. The symbols indicating approximate overlap must be replaced in an application by declared overlap thresholds or linkage relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The federation alignment taxonomy classifies clients according to which entities, feature coordinates, and tasks they share. Horizontal federation uses a common feature and task space across mostly different entities. Vertical federation uses overlapping entities whose attributes are split across clients. Transfer or task-heterogeneous federation has limited alignment or distinct tasks and therefore needs an explicit relation connecting representations or objectives. Any use of approximate overlap requires an application-specific threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Classification is determined by the overlap signature \((\{R_i\},\{C_i\},\{T_i\})\), not merely by the number or type of clients.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Horizontal alignment is often called sample-partitioned federation, while vertical alignment is often called feature-partitioned federation.
special_cases_latex: If all clients have identical \(C_i\) and \(T_i\) and pairwise disjoint \(R_i\), the federation is purely horizontal.
If all clients share the same linked entities and the feature blocks partition \(C\), the federation is purely vertical.
immediate_consequences_latex: Vertical federation requires entity alignment before losses involving joined feature vectors can be evaluated.
boundary_notes: Real deployments may be hybrid and need not belong uniquely to one class.
Feature alignment is distinct from equality of feature distributions.

notation.meaning: entity, feature-coordinate, and task-coordinate sets of client i

review_flags: No inspected source supports the precise taxonomy and overlap conventions.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-feature-task alignment taxonomy
Horizontal Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share the same feature and label schema but hold different observational units, so training aggregates objectives across row-partitioned data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is horizontal when every client records the same feature-label schema \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\), while clients hold distinct observational units. Formally, client \(i\) owns
\[D_i=\{(x_{ik},y_{ik}):k\in I_i\}\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y,\]
with aligned coordinates across clients and typically disjoint identifier sets \(I_i\cap I_j=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Training minimizes an aggregate such as \(F(w)=\sum_i p_i|I_i|^{-1}\sum_{k\in I_i}\ell(w;x_{ik},y_{ik})\) without transferring the records in \(D_i\).
assumptions_latex: All clients use a common feature space \(\mathcal X\), label space \(\mathcal Y\), and model parameter \(w\).
Client record identifiers are aligned sufficiently to determine whether units overlap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Horizontal federation represents a row-wise partition of a common-schema learning dataset.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by feature schema but partitioned by observational units.

notation.meaning: record identifiers held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the horizontal-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: common features with differing sample identities is the conventional horizontal partition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the row-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the exact definition, including the typical disjointness condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients share entity identities but hold different feature columns, jointly evaluating a model whose loss depends on the combined feature blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is vertical when clients describe overlapping entities but hold different feature blocks. For a shared identifier set \(I\), client \(i\) holds \(x_k^{(i)}\in\mathcal X_i\) for entity \(k\in I\), and the complete covariate is
\[x_k=(x_k^{(1)},\ldots,x_k^{(m)})\in\mathcal X_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal X_m.\]
Labels may be held by one designated client. The parties jointly minimize a loss depending on the combined feature blocks while neither raw block nor entity-level records are centrally pooled.
assumptions_latex: A privacy-preserving entity-alignment procedure identifies the common set \(I\).
Feature blocks have a specified common model and loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Vertical federation represents a column-wise feature partition over aligned entities.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation aligned by entities but partitioned by feature coordinates.

notation.meaning: features of entity k held by client i

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the vertical-federation taxonomy.
standard_field_rationale: shared entities with differing feature blocks is the conventional vertical partition.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits this taxonomy leaf and the feature-partition interpretation is standard, but no authoritative citation with a specific locator supports the stated entity-alignment and label-placement formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Transfer Federation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients with mismatched samples and feature spaces collaborate through a shared representation or transfer term rather than direct row or column alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federation is a transfer federation when participating clients have limited overlap in both observational units and feature spaces, so neither a common-schema horizontal partition nor an entity-aligned vertical partition applies. Client \(i\) has data from \(P_i\) on \(\mathcal X_i\times\mathcal Y_i\), and collaboration uses learned maps \(T_i:\mathcal X_i\to\mathcal Z\) or shared parameters to transfer information through a common representation space \(\mathcal Z\). The optimized objective couples client-specific prediction losses with an explicit cross-domain transfer or representation-alignment term.
assumptions_latex: At least two clients lack both complete entity alignment and a common feature schema.
A specified transfer map, shared representation, or cross-domain coupling relates their learning tasks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transfer federation couples otherwise nonaligned client domains through an explicit transferable representation or parameter relation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Federation requiring transfer across mismatched sample and feature domains.

notation.meaning: client-specific map into a shared representation

review_flags: Transfer-federation definitions vary, and no directly supporting locator was supplied.
The exact required transfer mechanism needs authoritative source confirmation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the taxonomy leaf, but transfer-federation terminology is not uniform. No source supports the asserted requirement of learned maps, shared representations, or an explicit alignment term, so the mathematical scope cannot be validated reliably.

children.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
children.top_down_role: Federated objectives optimized without a permanent central aggregator.

knowledge_statements.title: Decentralized Federated Optimization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clients optimize local objectives and enforce model consensus through peer-to-peer communication on a connected graph, without a permanent central aggregator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected client communication graph. Decentralized federated optimization solves
\[\min_{w_1,\ldots,w_m}\ \sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w_i)\quad\text{subject to}\quad w_i=w_j\ \text{for every }\{i,j\}\in E,\]
where client \(i\) evaluates \(F_i\) from its local data and exchanges model-derived messages only with graph neighbors. No permanent central aggregator computes the global update. Connectivity makes edge consensus equivalent to a common model \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), recovering the weighted federated objective.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is connected and undirected.
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
Each \(F_i\) is defined on a common parameter space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasible points satisfy \(w_1=\cdots=w_m\), reducing the problem to \(\min_w\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consensus formulation of a federated objective without a permanent central server.
review_flags: source_fulltext_pending
The source supports graph-consensus optimization; federated terminology remains to be checked.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The graph-consensus formulation is mathematically coherent and the definition role fits the leaf. However, the cited section supports decentralized graph-consensus optimization rather than the stronger federated characterization involving local data and absence of a permanent aggregator. A federated-optimization source with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Federated Coordinator Architectures
children.top_down_role: Coordinator-mediated optimization with persistent data locality and heterogeneous participation.

knowledge_statements.title: Federated Coordination Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinator optimizes a weighted client objective using messages from varying participant subsets, while each client's samples remain local.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The federated coordination boundary for \(\min_x F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\), is the interface under which a coordinator broadcasts \(x^t\) and participating client \(i\in S_t\) returns \(M_i^t=\Phi_i(x^t;P_i,\xi_i^t)\). The coordinator updates \(x^{t+1}=\Psi_t(x^t,\{M_i^t:i\in S_t\})\). Persistent data locality means that samples from \(P_i\) remain at client \(i\); heterogeneous participation permits \(S_t\) and the local maps \(\Phi_i\) to vary across clients and rounds.

At round \(t\), only clients in \(S_t\) participate.

children.title: Federated Optimization Assumptions and Heterogeneity
children.top_down_role: Client differences and participation processes that shape federated optimization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For clients \(i\in\mathcal I\), let \(f_i\) be local objectives, \(M_i\) local model spaces, \(R_{i,t}\) resource states, and \(I_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) participation indicators.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint specification of statistical, model, systems, and participation variability affecting a federated optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A federated client-variability regime is the joint family \(\mathcal V=\{(f_i,M_i,(R_{i,t})_{t\ge0},(I_{i,t})_{t\ge0}):i\in\mathcal I\}\) together with quantitative bounds or probability laws governing variation across clients and time. Statistical variability concerns differences among \(f_i\) or their data laws; model variability concerns differences among \(M_i\) or client prediction maps; systems variability concerns compute, memory, energy, bandwidth, delay, or availability encoded by \(R_{i,t}\); participation variability concerns the joint law of \(I_{i,t}\). A regime is homogeneous along a coordinate only when the corresponding client objects are identical or satisfy the declared zero-variability condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A client-variability regime records the client objectives, model spaces, time-varying resource states, and participation indicators, together with mathematical bounds or laws describing their variation. This separates statistical heterogeneity from model, systems, and participation heterogeneity. The regime is not a single scalar unless a particular metric has been chosen; each coordinate requires its own declared comparison rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal V\) determines which client differences and participation processes are admitted by an analysis or algorithmic guarantee.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A parameterized regime may be summarized by a vector \((\zeta_{\mathrm{stat}},\zeta_{\mathrm{model}},\zeta_{\mathrm{sys}},\zeta_{\mathrm{part}})\) once each component metric is explicitly defined.
special_cases_latex: The fully homogeneous full-participation regime has identical local objectives and model spaces, constant resource states, and \(I_{i,t}=1\) for all \(i,t\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A guarantee stated for one variability coordinate need not cover variation in the other coordinates.
boundary_notes: The four coordinates may be statistically dependent.

Statistical Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Statistical heterogeneity occurs when at least two clients have different data-generating distributions, regardless of how many samples each client holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let client \(i\) draw observations \(\xi\) from a probability distribution \(P_i\) on a common measurable sample space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\). The federation has statistical heterogeneity when the family \(\{P_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is not constant, equivalently when there exist clients \(i\ne j\) and an event \(A\in\mathcal A\) such that \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). This may reflect differing covariate, label, conditional, or joint distributions, independently of unequal client sample counts.
assumptions_latex: All \(P_i\) are probability measures on the same measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists i\ne j\) with \(P_i\ne P_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability arising from unequal local data-generating distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective heterogeneity is gradient disagreement between client objectives and their weighted aggregate; its weighted squared norm gives a pointwise quantitative measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let differentiable client objectives \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) have weights \(p_i\ge0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and let \(F(w)=\sum_i p_iF_i(w)\). Their objective heterogeneity at \(w\) is measured by
\[H(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i\|\nabla F_i(w)-\nabla F(w)\|^2.\]
The objectives are heterogeneous on a domain \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) when \(H(w)>0\) for some \(w\in W\); a uniform heterogeneity bound is \(H(w)\le B^2\) for every \(w\in W\).
assumptions_latex: Each \(F_i\) is differentiable on \(W\subseteq\mathbb R^d\).
\(p_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(w)\ge0\), and \(H(w)=0\) exactly when every positive-weight client gradient equals \(\nabla F(w)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Client variability measured by disagreement among local objective gradients.
review_flags: Several inequivalent objective-heterogeneity measures exist, and no supporting locator was supplied.
The selected gradient-dissimilarity convention requires source confirmation.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, but objective heterogeneity has several inequivalent conventions. No source supports this particular weighted gradient-disagreement measure or the proposed uniform bound, so the selected mathematical version requires authoritative confirmation.

knowledge_statements.title: Client Sample-Weight Imbalance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unequal client sample counts create unequal sample-proportional objective weights; the largest-to-smallest count ratio quantifies the imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose client \(i\) holds \(n_i\ge1\) observations and its empirical objective is \(F_i(w)=n_i^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}\ell(w;\xi_{ik})\). Sample-proportional aggregation assigns
\[p_i=\frac{n_i}{N},\qquad N=\sum_{j=1}^m n_j,\qquad F(w)=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iF_i(w).\]
Client sample-weight imbalance occurs when the weights are nonuniform, equivalently when some \(n_i\ne n_j\). It may be summarized by \(R=n_{\max}/n_{\min}\ge1\), with exact balance precisely when \(R=1\).
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many clients and every sample count satisfies \(n_i\ge1\).
The aggregate empirical risk weights every observation equally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sample-weight imbalance holds exactly when \((p_1,\ldots,p_m)\ne(1/m,\ldots,1/m)\), equivalently \(R>1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unequal empirical-objective weights induced by unequal client sample sizes.

notation.meaning: number of observations at client i

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this client-weight convention.
standard_field_rationale: sample-proportional empirical-risk weighting is standard, but other federation objectives may choose different weights.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf and the equivalences are correct under sample-proportional aggregation. Because federated objectives may use weights not induced by sample counts, an authoritative source with a specific locator is required to support this exact convention and scope.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Client Distribution Shift
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cross-client distribution shift occurs when at least two clients have different data distributions on the same measurable sample space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Cross-client distribution shift is the condition
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ P_i\ne P_j,
\]
equivalently, there exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) with \(P_i(A)\ne P_j(A)\). For a common loss, the induced objectives are \(F_i(x)=\int_{\mathcal Z}\ell(x;z)\,dP_i(z)\). Distribution shift need not imply \(F_i\ne F_j\), because distinct measures can yield identical expectations for the chosen loss class; conversely, the condition concerns the data-generating measures themselves.
assumptions_latex: Clients are indexed by \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and client \(i\) draws data from a probability measure \(P_i\) on a common measurable space \((\mathcal Z,\mathcal A)\).
A common measurable loss \(\ell:X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R\) induces \(F_i(x)=\mathbb E_{Z\sim P_i}[\ell(x;Z)]\) whenever the expectation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cross-client distribution shift holds exactly when \(P_i\ne P_j\) for some clients \(i,j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributional, rather than merely objective-value, heterogeneity on a shared sample space.

knowledge_statements.title: Systems Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systems heterogeneity means that clients differ over time in compute, memory, energy, communication capacity, latency, or availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
r_i(t)=(c_i(t),m_i(t),e_i(t),b_i(t),a_i(t))\in\mathcal R
\]
record client \(i\)'s compute capacity, memory, energy budget, bandwidth or latency characteristics, and availability at time \(t\). The federation has systems heterogeneity on a relevant time set \(T\) when
\[
\exists i\ne j,\ 
exists t\in T:\ r_i(t)\ne r_j(t).
\]
The definition permits deterministic, stochastic, and time-varying profiles and does not require the clients' data distributions or objectives to differ.
assumptions_latex: At time \(t\), client \(i\) has a resource-and-availability profile \(r_i(t)\) in a common profile space \(\mathcal R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Systems heterogeneity holds when \(r_i(t)\ne r_j(t)\) for some clients and relevant time.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-dependent device and communication variability, independent of statistical data differences.

notation.meaning: Compute, memory, energy, communication, and availability profile of client i

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Systems heterogeneity is cross-client or temporal nonidentity of the resource processes \(\{R_{i,t}\}\). Given a task requiring \(u_{i,t}\) compute operations, \(s_{i,t}\) memory, \(v_{i,t}\) energy, and \(q_{i,t}\) communicated bits, client \(i\) is operationally feasible at round \(t\) only if \(a_{i,t}=1\), \(s_{i,t}\le m_{i,t}\), \(v_{i,t}\le e_{i,t}\), and its compute and communication complete within the declared deadline, for example \(u_{i,t}/c_{i,t}+q_{i,t}/b_{i,t}+\delta_{i,t}\le D_t\). A systems-heterogeneity regime specifies the admissible set or joint law of these resource vectors rather than assuming identical clients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Systems heterogeneity is variation across clients or time in computation, memory, energy, bandwidth, latency, and availability. A local task is feasible only when the client is available, its memory and energy requirements fit its budgets, and its compute-plus-communication time meets the declared deadline. A rigorous regime specifies admissible resource vectors or their probability law; merely saying that devices are different is not a mathematical condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible participant set at round \(t\) consists of clients whose resource vector satisfies every declared task constraint.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A straggler model may encode systems heterogeneity through random completion times \(T_{i,t}\), with participation accepted only when \(T_{i,t}\le D_t\).
special_cases_latex: Homogeneous synchronous clients have identical deterministic \(R_{i,t}=R\) and a common deadline.
immediate_consequences_latex: Client selection based on completion feasibility can correlate participation with device type or data distribution.
boundary_notes: Systems heterogeneity does not mean statistical heterogeneity, although the two may be correlated.

knowledge_statements.title: Model Heterogeneity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model heterogeneity occurs when clients use distinct architectures or parameter spaces but retain a defined shared coordination or prediction interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A federation is model-heterogeneous when its clients use local model classes \(\mathcal H_i=\{h_{i,\theta}:\theta\in\Theta_i\}\) for which
\[
\exists i\ne j:\ (\Theta_i,\mathcal H_i)\ne(
\Theta_j,\mathcal H_j),
\]
while a common coordination interface remains available. Such an interface may be a variable \(z\in Z\) with client realizations \(D_i(z)\in\Theta_i\), a shared representation, or comparable predictions in \(\mathcal Y\). Direct coordinatewise parameter averaging is defined only when compatible embeddings into a common vector space have been specified.
assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) optimizes parameters \(\theta_i\in\Theta_i\) and produces outputs in a common prediction space \(\mathcal Y\).
Federated coordination is expressed through a common variable \(z\in Z\) and client-specific maps \(D_i:Z\to\Theta_i\), or through an equivalent shared prediction-level constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Model heterogeneity holds when the local model classes or parameterizations are not all identical while a common coordination interface remains defined.

knowledge_statements.title: participation rate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The participation rate is the fraction of eligible clients whose updates enter a round; its conditional expectation equals the average client inclusion probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In round \(t\), let \(E_t\) be the nonempty set of eligible clients and \(S_t\subseteq E_t\) the clients whose updates are included by the server. The realized participation rate is \(q_t=|S_t|/|E_t|\). Before selection, its conditional expected value is \(\bar q_t=\mathbb{E}[|S_t|\mid\mathcal H_t]/|E_t|=|E_t|^{-1}\sum_{i\in E_t}\mathbb{P}(i\in S_t\mid\mathcal H_t)\). Uniformly sampling exactly \(m_t\) eligible clients gives \(q_t=\bar q_t=m_t/|E_t|\).
assumptions_latex: \(S_t\subseteq E_t\) is measurable after the round's selection and response events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q_t=\frac{|S_t|}{|E_t|},\qquad \bar q_t=\frac{1}{|E_t|}\sum_{i\in E_t}\mathbb{P}(i\in S_t\mid\mathcal H_t).\]

children.title: Participation-Fairness Distortion Limitations
children.top_down_role: Objective distortions caused by nonrepresentative participation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let clients be indexed by \(i\in[M]\), let \(F_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), and let the intended federated objective be \(F_p(x)=\sum_{i=1}^M p_iF_i(x)\), where \(p\in\Delta_M\). In round \(t\), participation and aggregation induce random effective weights \(Q_t=(Q_{t,1},\ldots,Q_{t,M})\in\Delta_M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-client federated optimization with possibly nonrepresentative random participation; the definition concerns objective distortion, independently of any convergence theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(q_i=\mathbb E[Q_{t,i}]\) for a stationary participation rule and \(F_q(x)=\sum_i q_iF_i(x)\). The participation-fairness distortion on \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is \(\mathcal D_X(p,q)=\sup_{x\in X}|F_q(x)-F_p(x)|\). For tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), the rule lies on the \(\delta\)-distortion boundary when \(\mathcal D_X(p,q)=\delta\), is admissible when \(\mathcal D_X(p,q)\le\delta\), and is participation-fair when \(q=p\), equivalently \(\mathbb E[Q_{t,i}]=p_i\) for every client.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intended client weights define one objective, while expected participation and aggregation weights define an effective objective. Their worst-case absolute difference over the domain is the participation-fairness distortion. A rule is fair when every expected effective client weight equals its intended weight; a tolerance boundary is the level set where distortion equals the prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal D_X(p,q)=\sup_{x\in X}|\sum_i(q_i-p_i)F_i(x)|\), with fairness condition \(q=p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If every \(F_i\) is differentiable, a gradient-level analogue is \(\mathcal G_X(p,q)=\sup_{x\in X}\|\sum_i(q_i-p_i)\nabla F_i(x)\|\); it is a separate distortion metric, not generally equivalent to \(\mathcal D_X=0\).
special_cases_latex: If clients are sampled with probabilities \(\pi_i>0\) and an unbiased Horvitz--Thompson aggregation is used, then the effective mean weights can satisfy \(q_i=p_i\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncorrected unequal participation reweights client objectives by their participation probabilities and can move stationary points away from those of the intended objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under uncorrected participation, client \(i\)'s long-run exposure is proportional to \(p_iq_i\). Normalizing gives
\[
\widetilde p_i=\frac{p_iq_i}{\sum_{j=1}^np_jq_j},
\qquad
\widetilde F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde p_iF_i(x).
\]
Thus \(\widetilde F=F\) whenever all \(q_i\) are equal. If the \(q_i\) are unequal and
\[
\sum_i(\widetilde p_i-p_i)\nabla F_i(x)\ne0
\]
at some differentiability point \(x\), the effective and intended objective gradients differ there, exhibiting participation-induced objective bias.

knowledge_statements.title: Client-Level Fairness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under loss parity, a model is client-fair when the largest difference between any clients' losses is at most the chosen tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the client-loss-parity sense, define the disparity
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)=
\max_{1\le i\le n}F_i(x)-
\min_{1\le i\le n}F_i(x).
\]
A model \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-client-fair when
\[
\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)\le\varepsilon.
\]
The case \(\varepsilon=0\) requires equal loss for every client. This condition evaluates disparity across clients and is distinct from minimizing the weighted mean \(\sum_i p_iF_i(x)\), which alone imposes no bound on \(\Delta_{\mathrm{client}}(x)\).
assumptions_latex: Each client has a finite real-valued loss \(F_i(x)\) at the evaluated model \(x\in X\).
A tolerance \(\varepsilon\ge0\) is fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Group Representation Fairness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Group representation fairness requires each group's long-run participation exposure to remain within a tolerance of its declared target share.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The realized representation of group \(G\in\mathcal G\) is
\[
R_G=\sum_{i\in G}\rho_i.
\]
For prescribed target shares \(\pi_G\), group representation is \(\varepsilon\)-fair when
\[
\max_{G\in\mathcal G}|R_G-\pi_G|\le\varepsilon.
\]
Exact representation fairness corresponds to \(\varepsilon=0\). The targets may encode population shares, objective weights, or another declared policy, but they must be fixed independently of the realized participation whose fairness is being assessed.

knowledge_statements.title: Fairness under Unequal Availability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-availability selection realizes target client exposure only when no client's requested marginal exposure exceeds its availability probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unconditional exposure of client \(i\) is \(q_is_i\). Exact availability-adjusted fairness with target shares \(p_i\) and expected budget \(m\) requires
\[
q_is_i=mp_i\quad\text{for every }i.
\]
Consequently the unique marginal correction is
\[
s_i=\frac{mp_i}{q_i}.
\]
A valid policy with \(s_i\in[0,1]\) exists if and only if \(mp_i\le q_i\) for every \(i\). If this inequality fails, the target exposure is unattainable without reducing \(m\), relaxing the targets, or changing availability.
assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) is available with marginal probability \(q_i>0\), has target exposure \(p_i>0\), and \(\sum_i p_i=1\).
When available, client \(i\) is selected with conditional probability \(s_i\in[0,1]\), and the expected participation budget is \(m\in(0,\sum_iq_i]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact target exposure with budget \(m\) is feasible exactly when \(mp_i\le q_i\) for every client, using \(s_i=mp_i/q_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal-exposure feasibility under unequal availability and a fixed expected participation budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Federated SGD
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Federated SGD aggregates one stochastic gradient from each selected client and corrects by the client's history-conditional inclusion probability, yielding the intended objective gradient in conditional expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in X\), stepsizes \(\eta_t>0\), weights \(p_i\), and a horizon \(T\), round \(t\) samples \(S_t\). Each \(i\in S_t\) draws \(\xi_{i,t}\) and returns \(g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t})\). The server forms
\[
G_t=\sum_{i\in S_t}\frac{p_i}{q_{i,t}}g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t}),
\qquad
x_{t+1}=x_t-\eta_tG_t.
\]
Under the stated history-conditional inclusion and oracle-unbiasedness assumptions,
\[
\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=\nabla F(x_t).
\]
Stop after \(T\) rounds and output \(x_T\), or a prespecified average of the iterates.
assumptions_latex: The parameter domain \(X\) is a real vector space, \(p_i>0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\), and the differentiable objective is \(F(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iF_i(x)\).
Before sampling at round \(t\), the history \(\mathcal H_t\) contains \(x_t\), and \(q_{i,t}=\mathbb P(i\in S_t\mid\mathcal H_t)>0\).
For every client selected at round \(t\), \(\mathbb E[g_i(x_t;\xi_{i,t})\mid\mathcal H_t,\,i\in S_t]=\nabla F_i(x_t)\), and the displayed conditional expectations exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned iterate is generated by an inclusion-corrected stochastic-gradient update satisfying \(\mathbb E[G_t\mid\mathcal H_t]=\nabla F(x_t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-local-gradient, history-conditionally inclusion-corrected version of federated SGD.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication regimes are determined by whether the number of local updates between averaging events is one, uniformly bounded, or unbounded over time.

A communication-interval schedule is a sequence \((K_r)_{r\ge0}\) of positive integers. It is unit-communication when \(K_r=1\) for all \(r\), bounded-period when

T_R=
\sum_{r=0}^{R-1}K_r,

R(T)=
\max\{R:T_R\le T\}.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Client \(i\) participates in round \(t\) with indicator \(I_{t,i}\), inclusion probability \(\pi_{t,i}=\Pr(I_{t,i}=1)>0\), target weight \(p_i\), local-step count \(K_{t,i}\), and returned displacement \(\Delta_{t,i}\in\mathbb R^d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A linear federated update calibration rule chooses measurable coefficients \(w_{t,i}\) and optionally normalization maps \(N_{t,i}\) and forms \(\widehat\Delta_t=\sum_{i=1}^M I_{t,i}w_{t,i}N_{t,i}(\Delta_{t,i})\), followed by \(x_{t+1}=x_t+\gamma_t\widehat\Delta_t\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calibration rule transforms and reweights client displacements before aggregation. knowledge_statements.title: Federated Update Calibration Family
Normalized Client Updates
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide each client displacement by its accumulated local step size. The result is an average direction whose scale does not grow mechanically with local step count.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At round \(t\), client \(i\) initializes \(y_{i,0}=x_t\) and performs \(\tau_i\ge1\) steps
\[y_{i,k+1}=y_{i,k}-\eta_{i,k}g_{i,k},\qquad 0\le k<\tau_i.\]
Its displacement is \(\Delta_i=x_t-y_{i,\tau_i}=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau_i-1}\eta_{i,k}g_{i,k}\). Given a positive normalizer \(a_i=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau_i-1}\eta_{i,k}\), the normalized client update is
\[u_i=\frac{\Delta_i}{a_i}=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau_i-1}\frac{\eta_{i,k}}{a_i}g_{i,k}.\]
Thus \(u_i\) is a step-size-weighted average direction; for constant \(\eta_{i,k}=\eta_i\), it equals \(\tau_i^{-1}\sum_k g_{i,k}\).
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_i\ge1\) and \(\eta_{i,k}>0\).
All local iterates and directions lie in the same Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_i=\Delta_i/a_i\) is a convex combination of the local directions \(g_{i,k}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization converts variable-length local model displacements into average local directions.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: normalization follows directly from telescoping local descent steps

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Work Reweighting
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weight each displacement inversely by its local steps and step size, then apply the intended client weight. This prevents extra local work from automatically increasing client influence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let client \(i\) have target weight \(p_i\), local length \(\tau_i\), constant step size \(\eta_i>0\), and displacement \(\Delta_i=\eta_i\sum_{k=0}^{\tau_i-1}g_{i,k}\). The target-weighted average of client-average directions has the representation
\[\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\left(\frac1{\tau_i}\sum_{k=0}^{\tau_i-1}g_{i,k}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{p_i}{\eta_i\tau_i}\Delta_i.\]
Hence a server step \(x^+=x-\gamma\sum_i p_i\Delta_i/(\eta_i\tau_i)\) removes the purely multiplicative influence of unequal local step counts and step sizes while retaining the prescribed client weights.
assumptions_latex: Client \(i\) uses a constant local step size \(\eta_i\) during the round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i p_i\tau_i^{-1}\sum_k g_{i,k}=\sum_i p_i\Delta_i/(\eta_i\tau_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reweighting separates intended client importance from heterogeneous amounts of local work.

notation.meaning: intended objective weight of client i

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The displayed representation is exact for constant client-specific step sizes, and representation is an acceptable role here. A source is required for the claimed federated local-work calibration interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Probability Correction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide each participating client’s target-weighted update by its inclusion probability. The aggregate is unbiased, provided every relevant client can be selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) be a random participating set with inclusion probabilities \(q_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)>0\). For fixed client vectors \(u_i\) and target weights \(p_i\), define
\[\widehat u=\sum_{i\in S}\frac{p_i}{q_i}u_i.\]
Then
\[\mathbb E[\widehat u]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_i.\]
This identity requires only the marginal inclusion probabilities; independence of client selections is unnecessary. If some \(q_i=0\) while \(p_i u_i\ne0\), no estimator based solely on observed participating updates can recover that missing term without additional structural information.
assumptions_latex: \(u_i\) is fixed, or conditionally fixed, when \(S\) is sampled.
\(q_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)>0\) whenever \(p_i u_i\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat u]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Client-Weight Calibration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An aggregate matches the intended client-weighted target for every possible update exactly when each server coefficient times its inclusion probability equals the target client weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a random client set with \(q_i=\mathbb P(i\in S)>0\), and let the server form \(\widehat u=\sum_{i\in S}a_i u_i\), where \(a_i\) is deterministic conditional on the sampling design. For arbitrary fixed vectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\), the calibration condition
\[\mathbb E[\widehat u]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_i\]
holds if and only if
\[q_i a_i=p_i\qquad\text{for every }i.\]
Thus \(a_i=p_i/q_i\). Under full participation, \(q_i=1\), this reduces to the prescribed objective weights \(a_i=p_i\).

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Client Sampling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose every fixed-size client subset with equal probability. Each client has inclusion probability m/n, and the sample mean estimates the population mean without bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\) clients and an integer \(m\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), uniform client sampling without replacement draws a subset \(S\) uniformly from all \(m\)-element subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Thus
\[\mathbb P(S=A)=\binom{n}{m}^{-1}\quad\text{for every }A\text{ with }|A|=m,\qquad \mathbb P(i\in S)=\frac mn.\]
For fixed vectors \(u_i\), the sample mean \(\widehat u=m^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}u_i\) satisfies
\[\mathbb E[\widehat u]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n u_i.\]
assumptions_latex: \(1\le m\le n\).
The vectors \(u_i\) are fixed, or conditionally fixed, before sampling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(i\in S)=m/n\) and \(\mathbb E[m^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}u_i]=n^{-1}\sum_i u_i\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(m\ge 1\) clients have differentiable local objectives \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), target weights \(p_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^m p_i=1\), and round-\(t\) information \(\mathcal I_t\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An information-aware client-sampling rule is a measurable map \(\Pi_t:\mathcal I_t\mapsto\mathcal P(2^{[m]})\) whose inclusion probabilities satisfy \(q_{i,t}>0\) whenever \(p_i>0\), and for which at least one \(q_{i,t}\) depends on an optimization-relevant statistic in \(\mathcal I_t\), such as \(f_i(x_t)\), \(\|g_{i,t}\|\), a loss decrease, uncertainty score, or an estimator of update variance. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An information-aware rule assigns a conditional distribution to the participating-client subset using currently available optimization or statistical information. Every target client must retain positive inclusion probability. When preservation of the target weighted update is part of the interface, each sampled update is multiplied by its target weight divided by its inclusion probability, yielding a conditionally unbiased aggregate.

knowledge_statements.title: Information-aware client sampling
Importance-Weighted Client Sampling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inverse-probability weighting preserves the target mean. When at least one weighted update is nonzero, sampling in proportion to weighted update norms minimizes the second moment; when all weighted updates vanish, every sampling distribution is optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\), and let \(u_i\in\mathbb R^d\) be fixed. Let \(q_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n q_i=1\), with \(q_i>0\) whenever \(p_i\lVert u_i\rVert>0\). Draw \(I\) with probabilities \(q_i\) and define
\[G=\frac{p_I}{q_I}u_I.\]
Then
\[\mathbb E[G]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_i,\qquad \mathbb E\lVert G\rVert^2=\sum_{i:q_i>0}\frac{p_i^2\lVert u_i\rVert^2}{q_i}.\]
Set \(Z=\sum_{j=1}^n p_j\lVert u_j\rVert\). If \(Z>0\), the second moment is minimized by
\[q_i=\frac{p_i\lVert u_i\rVert}{Z}\]
for indices with \(p_i\lVert u_i\rVert>0\), with zero probability assigned to the remaining indices. If \(Z=0\), the target and second moment are zero, and every sampling distribution is optimal.
assumptions_latex: \(u_i\in\mathbb R^d\), \(p_i\ge0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n p_i=1\).
\(q_i\ge0\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n q_i=1\), and \(q_i>0\) whenever \(p_i\lVert u_i\rVert>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[G]=\sum_i p_i u_i\); if \(Z>0\), the minimum second moment is attained by \(q_i\propto p_i\lVert u_i\rVert\), while if \(Z=0\), every sampling distribution is optimal.

\[q_i=\frac{s_i}{\sum_{j=1}^n s_j}.\]
Draw one client \(I\sim q\), obtain its update \(u_I\), and output \(G=(p_I/q_I)u_I\). For a minibatch of \(m\) independent draws, output the average of the \(m\) corrected vectors. Stop after the prescribed number of communication rounds and return the current server iterate. Conditional on the scores and client updates,
\[\mathbb E[G]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_i.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Loss-Aware Client Sampling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample high-loss clients more often while retaining exploration, then inverse-weight selected updates. Conditional unbiasedness is preserved when losses are fixed before selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At round \(t\), let \(\ell_{i,t}\ge0\) be a client loss estimate available before selection, choose \(\varepsilon>0\), and define
\[q_{i,t}=\frac{p_i(\ell_{i,t}+\varepsilon)}{\sum_{j=1}^n p_j(\ell_{j,t}+\varepsilon)}.\]
Draw \(I_t\sim q_t\), obtain update \(u_{I_t,t}\), and use \(G_t=(p_{I_t}/q_{I_t,t})u_{I_t,t}\) in the server update. Repeat until the round budget or stopping criterion is met. Conditional on the preselection history and fixed client updates,
\[\mathbb E[G_t]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_{i,t}.\]
The exploration constant ensures positive probability for every positively weighted client.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Bias Correction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logged preselection probabilities and inverse weights certify conditional unbiasedness. The certificate is invalid when relevant clients have zero probability or probabilities depend on post-selection information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[G_t=\frac{p_{I_t}}{q_{I_t,t}}u_{I_t,t}.\]
The verifiable identities \(q_{i,t}>0\) and
\[\sum_{i=1}^n q_{i,t}\frac{p_i}{q_{i,t}}u_{i,t}=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i u_{i,t}\]

\(q_{i,t}>0\) whenever \(p_i u_{i,t}\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Resource-Aware Client Selection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select only available clients whose total resource cost fits the round budget, optimize expected utility, and use inclusion-probability correction when preserving target weights is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At round \(t\), client \(i\) reports an availability indicator \(a_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\), resource cost \(c_{i,t}\ge0\), and utility score \(s_{i,t}\). Given budget \(B_t\), choose a distribution \(\pi_t\) supported on subsets

Return the server iterate after the stopping budget is exhausted.

\(\mathcal C_t\ne\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.title: Client-Selection Bias Correction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighting each selected client by the reciprocal of its inclusion probability yields an unbiased target aggregate, although rare clients can cause high variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the target aggregate be \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i g_i\), where \(p_i\ge 0\), \(\sum_i p_i=1\), and \(g_i\in\mathbb R^d\). Let \(S\) be a random client subset with inclusion probabilities \(\pi_i=\Pr(i\in S)>0\). The Horvitz--Thompson aggregate is \[\widehat g=\sum_{i\in S}\frac{p_i}{\pi_i}g_i.\] Regardless of dependence among client-selection indicators, \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=g\). Thus inverse-inclusion weighting removes first-order selection bias; its variance may nevertheless be large when some \(\pi_i\) are small.
assumptions_latex: \(g_i\) is integrable for every client \(i\).
\(\pi_i>0\) whenever \(p_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i g_i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Design-based correction for nonuniform or availability-dependent participation, conditional on the current history and fixed potential client updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A client-selection bias correction is a collection of aggregation coefficients \(w_{i,t}(S_t,\mathcal F_t)\) such that, for every client \(i\) with \(p_i>0\), \(q_{i,t}>0\) and \(\mathbb E[\mathbf1\{i\in S_t\}w_{i,t}\mid\mathcal F_t]=p_i\). The corrected aggregate is \(\widehat u_t=\sum_{i\in S_t}w_{i,t}u_{i,t}\), which consequently targets \(u_t\) conditionally for arbitrary fixed vectors \((u_{i,t})_{i=1}^m\). The canonical first-order-inclusion correction is \(w_{i,t}=p_i/q_{i,t}\), yielding \(\widehat u_t=\sum_{i\in S_t}(p_i/q_{i,t})u_{i,t}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bias correction reweights each observed client update so that its expected coefficient equals that client's target objective weight. Positive inclusion probability is required for every positively weighted target client. Dividing the target weight by the conditional inclusion probability is the canonical correction and makes the aggregate conditionally unbiased for any fixed collection of client updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat u_t\mid\mathcal F_t,(u_{i,t})_{i=1}^m]=\sum_{i=1}^m p_i u_{i,t}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Universal conditional unbiasedness for all \((u_{i,t})\) is equivalent to \(\mathbb E[\mathbf1\{i\in S_t\}w_{i,t}\mid\mathcal F_t]=p_i\) for every \(i\).
special_cases_latex: For one sampled client \(I_t\), the corrected aggregate is \((p_{I_t}/q_{I_t,t})u_{I_t,t}\).
If \(q_{i,t}=p_i\) under singleton sampling, no numerical reweighting is needed.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: There are \(m\) clients. Client \(i\) has a parameter \(x_i\in X_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{d_i}\), local loss \(f_i:X_i\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and weight \(p_i\ge0\) with \(\sum_i p_i=1\). Shared variables, if present, lie in \(Z\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

Local weighted losses are combined with a coupling term or coupling constraint that transfers information among clients.
